A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same meta-dynamical state-space modeling work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across reorganization and renumbering.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic-system experiments and motor-cortex data analyses, including reconstruction, forecasting, few-shot transfer, and supplementary analyses.

after.justification: V2 retains these original results and adds CEBRA and LFADS comparisons and experiments using alternative inference methods.

M1.justification: The core low-rank hypernetwork state-space model is retained. V2 Appendix D substantially extends its learning and inference procedures with embedding-conditioned VSMC and DVBF, including a modified VSMC objective and DVBF innovation inference through the dynamics model. Naming the original seqVAE implementation DKF is clarification.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same variable-speed limit-cycle, Hopf, and Duffing systems and Centre-Out/Maze motor recordings, including held-out sessions and subject T. The added comparisons and inference experiments operate within this existing coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds evaluated single-session LFADS with a controller on motor recordings, multi-session CEBRA on limit-cycle and motor data, and single-session controls using VSMC and DVBF. These appear in Figures 6, 10, 12, and 19; the original four comparator families remain.

E3.justification: The original splits, sample budgets, metrics, architectures, and forecast horizons are retained. Added experiments introduce two-stage CEBRA evaluation through post-hoc generative-model fitting and matched single-session versus pretrained-model comparisons under alternative inference schemes. These are additions to the evaluation design, not demonstrated reruns of the original experiments.

E4.justification: V2 adds a substantial test of whether embedding structure and few-shot transfer persist under VSMC and DVBF (Appendix D, Figure 12). Appendix B also analyzes CEBRA's inferred trajectories and learned dynamical failure. Existing rank, training-scale, model-mismatch, and embedding-interpolation analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report Table 1 with one standard error, describe three-seed pretraining with best-model selection for few-shot evaluation, and average the rank analysis over three seeds. V2 adds results using existing reporting practices, without documenting a new uncertainty-estimation or significance-testing procedure.

E6.justification: Tables 1 and 2 retain their numerical entries. V2 substantially expands the reported results with LFADS and CEBRA comparisons and VSMC/DVBF transfer curves. Section 5.2 newly reports negative forecasting R-squared for the CEBRA-based motor model, while Figure 12 shows few-shot benefits under alternative inference schemes. Figure 5 drops one illustrative session panel.

T1.justification: V2 Appendix D adds formal development absent from v1: an embedding-conditioned VSMC lower-bound derivation through marginalization and Jensen's inequality (Equations 19–30), plus the DVBF latent construction and objective (Equation 31). These extend the mathematical treatment beyond the original seqVAE objective.

C1.justification: The abstract and three introductory contributions retain their meaning. Section 6 adds the claim that few-shot performance is largely agnostic to the inference method, extending the conclusions beyond v1's demonstrated seqVAE setting.

C2.justification: V2 explains CEBRA's poor forecasting through a fixed-point-like structure causing slowing or noise-induced oscillations. It also explicitly leaves theoretical justification of the observed hypernetwork expressivity advantage to future work. Existing limitations concerning event alignment, embedding inference, and shared task structure remain.

D1.justification: V2 specifies the Gaussian embedding prior, minibatch averaging, causal smoothing, LFADS implementation, vector-field alignment, and embedding sampling for visualizations. These add reproducibility information without establishing changes to the original implementation. Appendix E.1 also introduces an inconsistent noise statement, appending R distributed as N(0, 0.01) after retaining R = 0.01I.

R1.justification: Section 4 adds focused comparisons with multitask and low-rank RNN research and sharpens distinctions from CEBRA and CS-VAE. New references support the inference extensions and LFADS implementation; the Galanti–Wolf citation is removed. The original meta-learning discussion survives in Appendix A, and the central novelty positioning remains.

P1.justification: Sections 3.1–3.2 receive substantial explanatory rewriting, and baseline descriptions are consolidated. The appendices are extensively reorganized: meta-learning discussion moves there, data-generation descriptions are separated from results, and a contents list is added. These structural changes extend beyond inserting the new experiments.

P2.justification: V2 adds CEBRA, alternative-inference, and inference-overview figures (10, 12, and 14). It redraws and annotates vector fields, simplifies Figure 5, expands comparator displays in Figures 6 and 19, and relocates numerous retained displays. Tables 1 and 2 preserve their numerical content.

improvement.justification: V1's principal comparisons rely on one inference framework. V2 substantially strengthens validation through LFADS/CEBRA comparisons and matched VSMC/DVBF experiments, supporting transfer across additional tested inference schemes. Added derivations and implementation and visualization details improve assessability. The broad inference-agnostic claim still exceeds a demonstration of equal performance, and Appendix E.1 introduces a noise-description inconsistency, but these limitations do not outweigh the stronger empirical support and transparency.
